profile.campus: San Antonio, Bexar County, Texas (CyrusOne San Antonio campus, SAT1)
profile.address: 9999 Westover Hills Boulevard, San Antonio, TX 78251
profile.reading:
Per CyrusOne's own campus page, SAT1, the company's original San Antonio facility (opened 2012), sits at 9999 Westover Hills Boulevard, San Antonio, TX 78251, publishing 110,000 sq ft and 9 MW of IT capacity.

CyrusOne's first San Antonio facility opened in 2012; per CyrusOne's own press release on its fifth San Antonio campus (SAT5-SAT6, broken ground January 2025 in Texas Research Park), the company had invested approximately $1 billion in capital to date across its San Antonio campuses as of that release, and describes SAT5-SAT6 itself as two buildings totaling 276,000 sq ft and 36 MW of IT capacity, figures that differ somewhat from an earlier operator-page-sourced figure of 175,000 sq ft/33 MW recorded for that campus elsewhere in this registry, a discrepancy noted rather than silently reconciled. The San Antonio Report, a local nonprofit newsroom, reported in 2026 that the city hosts more than 20 operational data centers with 59 more in various planning stages; CPS Energy, the municipally owned utility, supplies power to 21 of the existing facilities (generating roughly $110 million in revenue) and has projected future data center energy demand in the metro at approximately 26,000 megawatts, while flagging water use as a growing constraint: data centers currently draw about 0.1% of San Antonio Water System's drinking water, but planned new facilities have requested roughly 600 acre-feet of drinking water and 3,000 acre-feet of recycled water against a system that has capacity for only about 10,000 additional acre-feet before requiring upgrades.

CyrusOne's San Antonio growth mirrors a broader pattern across Texas, where absence of a state corporate income tax, relatively low land and construction costs compared to Northern Virginia or Silicon Valley, and CPS Energy's municipal-utility rate structure have made the metro attractive to colocation and hyperscale operators alike; San Antonio's data center footprint has grown alongside comparable buildouts in Dallas-Fort Worth (where CyrusOne's Carrollton facility, opened in 2012, was described by the company as the largest data center in Texas at the time) and Austin.

sources.title: San Antonio has over 20 data centers and more on the way

profile.facility_note: CyrusOne SAT1, San Antonio, Texas: the company's original 2012-opened San Antonio facility, 110,000 sq ft and 9MW.
profile.research_note: Cowork facility-page writer 2026-09-03: rebuilt from a 2026-09-02 legacy profile shape; added San Antonio Report's 2026 CPS Energy/SAWS coverage and CyrusOne's own SAT5-SAT6 press release (confirming SAT1 as the original 2012 San Antonio facility) as sources.

reading.body:
SAT1 is the original 2012-opened facility in CyrusOne's San Antonio campus, occupying 110,000 square feet with 9 MW of IT capacity. At an assumed density of 40 kW per rack common in colocation, 9 MW corresponds to roughly 225 racks, or about 1,800 individual accelerators at 5 kW per GPU. The campus qualifies to host PCI DSS, HIPAA, FISMA and SSAE 16 Type II workloads.

SAT1 ranks 14th among the 18 facilities in Texas with published capacity, holding 1.9% of the state's disclosed 468 MW of data center IT load. Texas has 133 mapped data center locations overall; most publish no power figure, so published capacity vastly understates total operational footprint. CyrusOne has invested approximately $1 billion across its five San Antonio campuses to date, with SAT1 representing its smallest installation.

The San Antonio metro now hosts more than 20 operational data centers with 59 additional facilities in planning stages. CPS Energy projects future metro demand at approximately 26,000 megawatts, but water availability has emerged as the harder constraint: planned new facilities have requested roughly 600 acre-feet of drinking water and 3,000 acre-feet of recycled water against a system capacity of only 10,000 additional acre-feet before requiring infrastructure upgrades. Current data center demand is negligible at 0.1% of municipal drinking water consumption.
